title: Super Green Canna-Pesto with Infused Olive Oil
h1: Bright Green Cannabis Pesto, Blended in Five Minutes
metaDescription: Blend a bright basil cannabis pesto with part canna-oil, dose it by the quarter cup, and keep it safely in the fridge or freezer in labeled portions.
excerpt: A fast basil pesto with canna-oil standing in for some of the olive oil, an easy dose per quarter cup, and fridge and freezer storage that keeps it safe.
keyTakeaways: THC in the canna-oil ÷ 4 = the dose in each quarter-cup serving.
Season with the plain olive oil first; the canna-oil goes in last.

body:
This cannabis pesto is a vivid green sauce for pasta, sandwiches and chicken that blends in about five minutes once the nuts are toasted. Canna-oil stands in for part of the olive oil, which makes the dose per serving easy to set.

## Dosing Your Cannabis Pesto

The batch makes about 1 cup, four quarter-cup servings, each carrying a quarter of the canna-oil's THC. Season with only the plain oil in, so you never taste-test the infused version. Keep infused pesto for adults 21 and older; as with other edibles, it may need 2 hours to take effect, so stop at one serving ([how to choose a dose](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/)).

## Ingredients

Basil leads, joined by garlic, parmesan, toasted walnuts or pine nuts, lemon and flat-leaf parsley. Home growers within [Michigan's home-grow limits](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) can swap fresh leaves in for the parsley; they add color, not a meaningful dose.

The oil is extra-virgin olive oil plus measured [canna-oil](/blog/canna-oil-recipe/). Need flower for a batch? Shop your local [High Society menu](/shop/) online and pick up in store or curbside.

## Blend It

Pulse the herbs, garlic, cheese, nuts and lemon to a coarse paste, stream in the plain oil, then taste and season. Add the canna-oil last and pulse just until blended, scraping the bowl. Serve it uncooked, tossed with hot pasta off the burner rather than fried.

## Storage and Labeling

Garlic and herbs held in oil need the fridge: the CDC advises refrigerating homemade garlic or herb oils and discarding them after 4 days, a sensible limit for pesto too. Cover the surface with a thin film of olive oil, label the jar with the dose per quarter cup and keep it apart from plain sauces.

## Ways to Use It

Measure first, then spoon. A quarter cup coats a plate of pasta with a splash of pasta water. A measured spoonful brightens a sandwich, eggs once they're off the heat, or vegetables straight from the oven. On another night, try our [fried sage cannabis gnocchi](/blog/fried-sage-cannabis-gnocchi/).

faq.q: Do raw cannabis leaves make pesto psychoactive?
faq.a: Not in any meaningful way. Uncooked cannabis carries its THC mostly in the acid form, THCA, which doesn't produce psychoactive effects in people unless heat converts it. Leaves also carry far less than flowers: one 2020 study measured about 1 to 2 percent total cannabinoids in leaves, versus roughly 16 to 20 percent in flowers. See our [THCA explainer](/blog/thc-vs-thca/).

Yes, and freezing keeps it far longer than the fridge. Spoon measured portions into an ice cube tray, freeze, then bag the cubes and write the dose per cube on the bag. Some cooks add the cheese after thawing for a fresher texture. Thaw portions in the fridge.

Yes. Toasted sunflower or pumpkin seeds give similar richness, or skip the nuts and add a little more parmesan. The dose doesn't change, since it comes from the canna-oil. Cooking for someone with a nut allergy? Check the seed and cheese labels too.

ingredients: ½ cup flat-leaf parsley, or fresh cannabis leaves if you grow your own
⅓ cup walnuts or pine nuts
¼ teaspoon salt, plus black pepper to taste
½ cup oil in total: your measured canna-oil plus extra-virgin olive oil (see the dosing note)
steps: Toast the nuts in a dry skillet over medium-low heat for 3 to 5 minutes, until fragrant. Let them cool.
Pulse the basil, parsley or leaves, garlic, parmesan, nuts, lemon juice and salt in a food processor until finely chopped.
With the motor running, stream in the plain olive oil. Taste and adjust the salt, pepper and lemon now.
Add the measured canna-oil and pulse 5 to 10 times, scraping the bowl, until evenly blended.
Divide into four quarter-cup portions. Serve right away, refrigerate for up to 4 days, or freeze.
recipe.dosingNote: **THC per quarter cup = THC in the canna-oil you add ÷ 4.** Your oil's ceiling in milligrams is the flower's weight in grams, times its THC share as a decimal (16% = 0.16), times 1,000. Say you infused 3.5 g of 16% flower into 1 cup of olive oil: that's no more than 560 mg, close to 35 mg in a tablespoon or 12 mg in a teaspoon. One teaspoon in this batch means at most about 3 mg per serving; one tablespoon, about 9 mg. Decarboxylation and infusion leave less THC than the math suggests, and fresh leaves add almost none. Start low with one serving, wait 2 hours, label every container, and keep the jar on a high shelf, clear of kids and pets.

claims.source: https://www.cdc.gov/cannabis/faq/index.html (WebFetch 2026-10-24): "it can take up to 2 hours to feel the effects from the drug"

claims.claim: Uncooked cannabis carries its THC mostly as THCA, which doesn't produce psychoactive effects in people unless heat converts it (FAQ); raw leaves add color, not a meaningful dose (body, takeaway, dosing note)
claims.source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28861488/ (Moreno-Sanz 2016, abstract via NCBI E-utilities): THCA-A "can represent up to 90% of the total THC contained in the plant"; it "does not elicit psychoactive effects in humans"; "Decarboxylation also occurs rapidly during baking of edibles, smoking, or vaporizing"

claims.claim: Leaves carry far less than flowers: one study found about 1 to 2 percent total THC in leaves, versus 10 to 12 percent in flowers (FAQ)
claims.fix: the 10-12% / 1-2% figures are not that study's findings: Jin et al. quote them in their introduction from a 2014 American Herbal Pharmacopoeia monograph; their own results were total cannabinoids, 1.10-2.10% in leaves versus 15.77-20.37% in inflorescences. Now "one 2020 study measured about 1 to 2 percent total cannabinoids in leaves, versus roughly 16 to 20 percent in flowers"
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7039888/ (Jin et al. 2020, Scientific Reports; full text via Europe PMC): results, "Total cannabinoids quantified in leaves were between 1.10% and 2.10%"; "Total cannabinoids quantified in inflorescence were between 15.77% and 20.37% in all three chemovars"; the introduction's "inflorescences (10–12%), leaves (1–2%)" cites ref. 29, Upton et al., American Herbal Pharmacopoeia, 2014

Dosing note: 3.5 g of 16% flower in 1 cup of oil is at most 560 mg, about 35 mg per tablespoon or 12 mg per teaspoon; 1 teaspoon in the batch is at most about 3 mg per serving, 1 tablespoon about 9 mg; decarboxylation and infusion leave less
claims.fix: wording: "Have one serving" became "Start low with one serving" so the note says to start low and wait (arithmetic checked: 560 ÷ 16 = 35; 35 ÷ 3 = 11.7; 11.7 ÷ 4 = 2.9; 35 ÷ 4 = 8.75)
claims.source: arithmetic; build contract section 4 recipe rule

review.notes: Independent fact-check: the CDC FAQ and the CDC botulism page were opened with WebFetch; the Moreno-Sanz 2016 abstract was read through NCBI E-utilities and Jin et al. 2020 through Europe PMC (full text, including its reference list). High Society facts used: order flower online for in-store or curbside pickup; no product said to be stocked, nothing implies High Society sells leaves, and no phone, hours, address, payment, prices, deals or app. Writer's notes: Fan leaves framed as a home-grower option only; nothing implies High Society sells leaves. The THCA source abstract also discusses therapeutic research; none of that is repeated, and the two source labels are shortened to leave out title words about therapy or medicine. Dose figures are ceilings from a labeled example.
